questions.prompt: Why can an NFA be easier to write down than a DFA for the same language, even though both accept exactly the regular languages?
questions.answer:
- An NFA may have several transitions per symbol and ε-transitions, so it can "guess" (e.g. where a suffix starts).
- A DFA must track every possibility explicitly in its states.
- Same power: every NFA can be turned into a DFA (powerset construction), possibly with exponentially many states.

questions.prompt: Explain when an NFA accepts a word, and how that differs from a DFA.
questions.answer:
- DFA: exactly one run; accept if it ends in a final state.
- NFA: accepts if **at least one** possible run ends in a final state after reading the whole word.
- Runs that get stuck (no transition) are simply discarded.

questions.prompt:
Which language does this DFA over {a, b} accept, and what does each state remember?

```automaton
start: q0
final: q2
q0 -b-> q0
q0 -a-> q1
q1 -a-> q1
q1 -b-> q2
q2 -a-> q1
q2 -b-> q0
```
questions.answer:
- All words that end in **ab**
- q0: nothing useful seen yet, q1: last symbol was a, q2: last two symbols were ab
- Typical mistake: "contains ab" (then q2 would never be left)

topics.title: Powerset construction
topics.notes: NFA → DFA, ε-closure, why at most 2^n states.

questions.prompt: Explain the idea of the powerset construction in your own words.
questions.answer:
- Each DFA state is a **set** of NFA states: all states the NFA could be in after the input so far.
- Start state: ε-closure of the NFA start state.
- Transition on a: union of the a-successors, then ε-closure.
- A set is final if it contains an NFA final state.
- Only reachable sets are built.

questions.prompt: What if the NFA has n states: how many states can the DFA have at most, and why is it usually far fewer in practice?
questions.answer:
- At most 2^n states (all subsets).
- Built from the start state, only **reachable** subsets appear, which is usually far fewer.
- There are languages where the exponential blow-up really happens (e.g. "the n-th symbol from the end is a").

topics.title: Regular expressions
topics.notes: Syntax, Thompson construction, state elimination DFA → regex.

questions.prompt: Write a regular expression over {a, b} for all words that contain "ab" at least once, and say how you would check it.
questions.answer:
- e.g. `(a|b)*ab(a|b)*`.
- Check: a word is in the language iff it has the substring ab; test examples like ab, bab, aab (yes) and ba, bbb, ε (no).

questions.prompt: Why does the language of a regular expression with a star always contain the empty word ε?
questions.answer:
- r* means zero or more repetitions of r.
- Zero repetitions give ε, so ε ∈ L(r*) for every r, even r = ∅.

questions.prompt: Explain what it means for two DFA states to be equivalent and how the table-filling algorithm finds them.
questions.answer:
- Equivalent: for every word w, both states either accept or reject after reading w.
- Mark all pairs (final, non-final) as distinguishable.
- Repeatedly mark a pair if some symbol leads to an already marked pair.
- Unmarked pairs at the end are equivalent and get merged.

questions.prompt: Why do you remove unreachable states before minimizing?
questions.answer:
- They never influence which words are accepted.
- Leaving them in can make the result not minimal (they may not merge with anything).
- Minimal DFA = no unreachable states and no two equivalent states.

topics.title: Pumping lemma for regular languages
topics.notes: Proof structure, typical mistakes when choosing w and the split.

questions.prompt: Explain how you use the pumping lemma to show that a language is not regular.
questions.answer:
- Assume L is regular with pumping length p.
- Choose a word w ∈ L with |w| ≥ p (cleverly, depending on p).
- For **every** split w = xyz with |xy| ≤ p and |y| ≥ 1, find an i with xy^iz ∉ L.
- Contradiction, so L is not regular.
- Typical mistake: picking one specific split instead of covering all of them.

questions.prompt: What if a language satisfies the pumping property: does that prove it is regular?
questions.answer:
- No. The lemma is only a necessary condition.
- Some non-regular languages can be pumped too.
- To prove regularity, give a DFA, NFA or regex (or use closure properties).
